lead: A digital transmitter sends one of M known waveforms in each symbol interval of T seconds. The receiver can treat each waveform as a point in a space of at most M dimensions, with axes built by the Gram-Schmidt procedure. Energy becomes squared length and the difference between two signals becomes a distance. The matched filter, the optimum detector and every error-probability formula later in this unit are geometry on that picture.
prereq: You need: integration of piecewise-constant signals, and vectors (dot product, length).

blocks.text: Two real signals x(t) and y(t) on 0 ≤ t ≤ T are compared by their inner product, the integral of their product:
Here the unit is V²·s when x and y are voltages. ⟨x, y⟩ = 0 means x and y are orthogonal.
The energy of x is Ex = ⟨x, x⟩, the energy it would deliver to a 1 Ω resistor, and its norm (length) is ‖x‖ = √Ex, in V·√s.

An orthonormal basis is a set of N functions φ1(t) … φN(t) with ⟨φi, φj⟩ = 1 when i = j and 0 otherwise. Each φ has unit energy, so when time is in ms its height is in 1/√ms. If every signal of the set is a weighted sum of the φ's,
Here smi is the i-th coordinate of signal m, in V·√s. The vector sm = (sm1, …, smN) is the signal's point.

Then all the integrals become vector arithmetic: the energy is E<sub>m</sub> = Σ<sub>i</sub> s<sub>mi</sub>² (the squared length), the inner product is the dot product, and the squared distance between two signals is d²<sub>mn</sub> = Σ<sub>i</sub>(s<sub>mi</sub> − s<sub>ni</sub>)² = ∫₀ᵀ [s<sub>m</sub>(t) − s<sub>n</sub>(t)]² dt.
Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization builds the basis from the signals themselves, one signal at a time. Each new signal keeps only the part that the axes found so far cannot explain.

items: First axis: φ<sub>1</sub> = s<sub>1</sub>/‖s<sub>1</sub>‖ (take the first signal with nonzero energy).
For the next signal s<sub>m</sub>, find its projection on every existing axis: c<sub>i</sub> = ⟨s<sub>m</sub>, φ<sub>i</sub>⟩.
Subtract them to get the residual: g<sub>m</sub>(t) = s<sub>m</sub>(t) − Σ<sub>i</sub> c<sub>i</sub> φ<sub>i</sub>(t).
If ‖g<sub>m</sub>‖ = 0, s<sub>m</sub> is a combination of the old axes: add no axis.
If ‖g<sub>m</sub>‖ ≠ 0, add the new axis φ = g<sub>m</sub>/‖g<sub>m</sub>‖.
Repeat for m = 2, 3, …, M. Each signal adds at most one axis, so the dimension N ≤ M.

blocks.text: The residual is orthogonal to every old axis: ⟨g<sub>m</sub>, φ<sub>k</sub>⟩ = ⟨s<sub>m</sub>, φ<sub>k</sub>⟩ − Σ<sub>i</sub> c<sub>i</sub>⟨φ<sub>i</sub>, φ<sub>k</sub>⟩ = c<sub>k</sub> − c<sub>k</sub> = 0, because only the term i = k survives. Taking the signals in a different order gives different axes and different coordinates, but the energies and the distances between points stay the same; they are properties of the waveforms, not of the axes.

sections.h3: Cauchy-Schwarz and the standard signal sets

blocks.text: No inner product can be larger than the product of the two lengths:
Here this is the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. Equality holds only when y(t) = c·x(t) for a constant c. It is the step that proves the matched filter is optimum (see the matched filter).

items: Binary antipodal (polar NRZ, BPSK): s2 = −s1. One axis, points +√E and −√E, distance 2√E.
On-off (unipolar): points 0 and √E on one axis, distance √E.
Binary orthogonal: ⟨s1, s2⟩ = 0 with equal energy E. Two axes, points (√E, 0) and (0, √E), distance √(2E).
M-ary PAM: one pulse shape p(t) and M amplitudes, so one axis φ1 = p/‖p‖ and M points on a line.

blocks.text: For the same energy antipodal points are farther apart (2√E) than orthogonal ones (√(2E)), so they give the lower error rate (see optimum detection). Carrier sets such as QPSK belong to digital passband modulation.

examples.question: Over 0 ≤ t ≤ 1 ms, s<sub>1</sub>(t) = 1 V for the whole interval, s<sub>2</sub>(t) = 2 V for the first half and 0 for the second, and s<sub>3</sub>(t) = 0 for the first half and 2 V for the second. Work in V·√ms. (a) Build the basis by Gram-Schmidt in the order s<sub>1</sub>, s<sub>2</sub>, s<sub>3</sub>. (b) Give the coordinates and energies. (c) Find the three distances. (d) Check Cauchy-Schwarz for s<sub>1</sub>, s<sub>2</sub>.
steps: Each half lasts 0.5 ms. E<sub>1</sub> = 1² × 1 = 1 V²·ms, so ‖s<sub>1</sub>‖ = 1 V·√ms and φ<sub>1</sub>(t) = s<sub>1</sub>/‖s<sub>1</sub>‖ = 1/√ms over the whole interval.
s<sub>2</sub>: c<sub>1</sub> = ⟨s<sub>2</sub>, φ<sub>1</sub>⟩ = 2 × 1 × 0.5 + 0 = 1 V·√ms. Residual g<sub>2</sub> = s<sub>2</sub> − 1·φ<sub>1</sub> = +1 V on the first half and −1 V on the second.
‖g<sub>2</sub>‖² = 1² × 0.5 + (−1)² × 0.5 = 1, so ‖g<sub>2</sub>‖ = 1 and φ<sub>2</sub>(t) = +1/√ms on the first half, −1/√ms on the second.

s<sub>3</sub>: ⟨s<sub>3</sub>, φ<sub>1</sub>⟩ = 2 × 0.5 = 1; ⟨s<sub>3</sub>, φ<sub>2</sub>⟩ = 0 × 0.5 + 2 × (−1) × 0.5 = −1. Residual g<sub>3</sub> = s<sub>3</sub> − φ<sub>1</sub> + φ<sub>2</sub> = (0 − 1 + 1, 2 − 1 − 1) = 0 on both halves. No new axis: s<sub>3</sub> = 2s<sub>1</sub> − s<sub>2</sub>, so N = 2 for M = 3.
Energies from coordinates: E<sub>1</sub> = 1, E<sub>2</sub> = 1 + 1 = 2, E<sub>3</sub> = 2 V²·ms. Check from the waveform: E<sub>2</sub> = 2² × 0.5 = 2.

Distances: d<sub>12</sub> = √(0² + 1²) = 1, d<sub>13</sub> = 1, d<sub>23</sub> = √(0² + 2²) = 2 V·√ms. Check d<sub>23</sub> from the waveforms: ∫(s<sub>2</sub> − s<sub>3</sub>)² = 2² × 0.5 + (−2)² × 0.5 = 4, so d<sub>23</sub> = 2.

Cauchy-Schwarz: ⟨s<sub>1</sub>, s<sub>2</sub>⟩ = 1 × 1 + 0 × 1 = 1 V²·ms, while ‖s<sub>1</sub>‖‖s<sub>2</sub>‖ = 1 × √2 = 1.414. 1 ≤ 1.414; not equal, because s<sub>2</sub> is not a multiple of s<sub>1</sub>.
examples.answer: Two axes, φ<sub>1</sub> = 1/√ms flat and φ<sub>2</sub> = ±1/√ms on the two halves; s<sub>1</sub> = (1, 0), s<sub>2</sub> = (1, 1), s<sub>3</sub> = (1, −1) V·√ms; energies 1, 2, 2 V²·ms; distances 1, 1 and 2 V·√ms.

traps: Assuming N = M. A signal that is a combination of earlier ones gives a zero residual and adds no axis; in the worked example M = 3 but N = 2.
Using the residual g<sub>m</sub> as an axis without dividing by ‖g<sub>m</sub>‖. Every later coordinate is then wrong.
Taking distance as a difference of energies. d² = Σ(s<sub>mi</sub> − s<sub>ni</sub>)²; s<sub>2</sub> and s<sub>3</sub> in the example have equal energy but are 2 V·√ms apart.
Expecting the coordinates to stay the same in another order. Start with s<sub>2</sub> and its point becomes (√2, 0); only energies and distances are fixed.
Giving answers without units, or giving an axis in volts. Coordinates are in V·√s, energies in V²·s and axis heights in 1/√s.

quiz.q: Define the inner product of two real signals on 0 ≤ t ≤ T, and state when they are orthogonal.
quiz.a: ⟨x, y⟩ = ∫₀ᵀ x(t)y(t) dt, in V²·s. They are orthogonal when ⟨x, y⟩ = 0.

quiz.q: Why can the dimension N be smaller than the number of signals M?
quiz.a: A signal that is a linear combination of the axes already built has a zero residual and adds no axis. In the worked example s<sub>3</sub> = 2s<sub>1</sub> − s<sub>2</sub>, so three signals need only two axes.

quiz.q: T = 2 ms. s<sub>1</sub>(t) = 1 V throughout; s<sub>2</sub>(t) = +1 V for the first ms and −1 V for the second. Find the basis, the coordinates and the distance.
quiz.a: E<sub>1</sub> = 2 V²·ms, φ<sub>1</sub> = s<sub>1</sub>/√2. ⟨s<sub>2</sub>, φ<sub>1</sub>⟩ = (1 − 1)/√2 = 0, so g<sub>2</sub> = s<sub>2</sub> and φ<sub>2</sub> = s<sub>2</sub>/√2. s<sub>1</sub> = (√2, 0), s<sub>2</sub> = (0, √2) V·√ms; d = √(2 + 2) = 2 V·√ms. The pair is orthogonal.

quiz.q: In the worked example, redo Gram-Schmidt in the order s<sub>2</sub>, s<sub>1</sub>. Find the new coordinates of s<sub>2</sub> and s<sub>1</sub> and check d<sub>12</sub>.
quiz.a: φ<sub>1</sub> = s<sub>2</sub>/√2 (height √2/√ms on the first half). s<sub>2</sub> = (√2, 0). ⟨s<sub>1</sub>, φ<sub>1</sub>⟩ = √2 × 0.5 = 0.707; residual = s<sub>1</sub> − 0.707φ<sub>1</sub> = 0 then 1 V, norm 0.707, so s<sub>1</sub> = (0.707, 0.707). d<sub>12</sub> = √((1.414 − 0.707)² + 0.707²) = √(0.5 + 0.5) = 1, as before.

quiz.q: All M signals of a set have energy E. Bound ⟨s<sub>m</sub>, s<sub>n</sub>⟩ and say what the two extreme cases mean for detection.
quiz.a: Cauchy-Schwarz gives −E ≤ ⟨s<sub>m</sub>, s<sub>n</sub>⟩ ≤ E. Since d² = 2E − 2⟨s<sub>m</sub>, s<sub>n</sub>⟩, the value +E (identical signals) gives d = 0 and they cannot be told apart, the worst case. The value −E (antipodal signals) gives the largest distance 2√E, the best case.

beyond: Choosing M points in N dimensions with the largest minimum distance for a given energy is the sphere-packing problem, and modern constellations (and lattice codes) are designed that way. In software, a numerically stable Gram-Schmidt is the QR decomposition, numpy.linalg.qr in Python. Search for QR decomposition, sphere packing and signal constellation design.

figure.caption: Left: the three waveforms of the worked example. Right: their points on the two Gram-Schmidt axes. s<sub>3</sub> = 2s<sub>1</sub> − s<sub>2</sub> adds no third axis, and the distances 1, 1 and 2 V·√ms can be read straight off the plane.
